# Ref_Auction Playbook

**On budget tracking:**
When I see my budget displayed alongside my bid, I will verify it immediately against my own running calculation: starting budget minus all previous winning bids equals my true remaining budget. In this episode, my budget display showed inconsistencies (20 to 974 to 991 to 982 to 966 to 16), which I now understand reflects the running total after each lot result is revealed. I must track not just bids I make, but which bids actually won and consumed budget. If I bid but don't win, my budget doesn't decrease. I will update my mental model each time a lot result is announced before moving to the next round.

**On initial lot evaluation:**
When a lot opens in round 1, I will compare my valuation to the estimate and current bid. If my value exceeds the estimate by a meaningful margin (15%+), I will bid to establish presence early rather than pass. Early bidding when I have a clear value advantage sets the tone and may discourage future competition. However, I will not bid recklessly on marginal value. A lot worth 34 on estimate 32 is strong; a lot worth 28 on estimate 31 is weak and I should pass.

**On aggressive bidding when ahead on value:**
When the current high bid is substantially below my valuation (more than 30% below), I will raise decisively to secure the lot rather than bidding minimally. Minimal bids in high-value situations invite counteroffers and waste the advantage. In this episode, lot 5 was worth 46 with current bid 12 (74% gap) and estimate 40—I bid 16 to establish strength, then bid 28 in round 2 to win at 28, netting +18. This is the correct approach for high-confidence opportunities.

**On continuation in round 2:**
When round 2 arrives and I'm already committed to a lot, I will bid to win if my valuation still exceeds the current bid by enough to profit after payment. I should complete the purchase if clear value remains. In this episode, lot 5 round 2 had current bid 24, my valuation 46—a +22 margin at current price—so bidding 28 to win was correct. However, I should recognize when I've already won a lot and not continue bidding on it. In this episode, after winning lot 2 at 18, I did not face a round 2 on that lot, which means the lot was settled and capital was locked in.

**On lots worth close to or below estimate:**
When a lot is worth 27-28 to me but carries an estimate of 31, I will pass. This signals the lot may not be strong value. I should only bid if the current price is very low relative to my valuation, not relative to the estimate. The gap between my value and the estimate is the red flag, not the gap between my value and current bid.

**On competitive positioning and avoiding shutout bias:**
I will track which bidders are winning lots and at what prices, but I must not let competitive anxiety drive me to bid on marginal lots just to "stay in the game." Accepting defeat on low-value lots is better than chasing bids that erode profit. In this episode, I won lots 2 and 5 decisively on strong value, finished +16. I should replicate this selectivity.

**On passing vs. bidding in early rounds:**
When a lot is worth less than the estimate by a wide margin (e.g., worth 15 on estimate 25), I will pass in round 1 even if the current bid is low. The estimate gap signals the lot is weak, and there is no guarantee the price will stay low in round 2.

**On budget allocation across the auction:**
I have a fixed total budget (1000 in this episode) and 5 lots to potentially win. I should not spend heavily on early lots and leave myself capital-constrained for later ones, especially if later lots offer better value. In this episode, I won lot 2 at 18 early, then had ample capital for lot 5. However, I should be mindful: if I win an early marginal lot at high price, I constrain my ability to pursue strong value later. Only bid decisively on high-confidence, high-margin opportunities.

**On final scoring:**
Winning 1–2 lots decisively at strong prices beats winning multiple marginal lots or losing money chasing value. Discipline and selective bidding on high-confidence opportunities maximizes final score. In this episode, I won 2 lots (2 and 5) at +18 profit each, totaling +36 profit. However, I note my final score was reported as +16, which suggests one of those wins may not have been counted or I made an arithmetic error in my own tracking. I will recalculate at the end of each episode to verify.

# Playbook for ref_auction

When I open the bidding on a lot with no prior bids, I bid the minimum raise to establish position while preserving budget.

When the standing bid is significantly below my valuation, I raise to lock in positive expected value, not just the minimum amount.

When deciding whether to continue bidding in a round, I calculate my net gain if I win at the next minimum raise: (my valuation - next bid amount). If this is positive, I bid.

I track my total winnings and spending so far to understand my position relative to other bidders, but I focus my decisions on individual lot value, not on trying to match or beat specific competitors.

When calculating remaining budget after a win, I subtract only the actual price paid from my starting budget. I do not guess at round numbers or assume I have money I haven't tracked. If uncertain about my remaining budget, I perform an explicit calculation from my known spending.

When a lot is in its final round (round 2/2), I'm more willing to bid to win if the value-to-me exceeds the standing bid, because there will be no further opportunity to acquire similar value.

I bid to win lots where I have positive expected value at the current price, measured by (my valuation - price I'd pay), regardless of whether other bidders have won more lots than me.

I should not bid aggressively in round 1/2 unless my valuation is significantly higher than the standing bid. In early rounds, I have another chance at the lot, so I can afford to pass and re-evaluate in round 2. This preserves budget for lots where I have stronger conviction or higher value.

When my valuation is close to or below the standing bid, I should pass rather than bid, even if the current price is still below my valuation. Low-margin wins tie up budget and limit optionality on future lots.

I should be willing to pass on a lot entirely if another bidder is willing to pay more than my true valuation, even if I'd break even or make a small profit. My goal is to maximize total score across all lots, not to win every lot with positive expected value.

I must carefully track my remaining budget after each win. If I spend money, I must subtract it from my available budget going forward. Large discrepancies between expected and actual remaining budget suggest tracking errors that will compound and distort my subsequent decisions.

On every lot in round 2/2, I should calculate whether the standing bid plus minimum raise leaves me with meaningful positive expected value (ideally more than the bare minimum). If the margin is too thin, I pass and accept that I won't win every lot.

# Auction Playbook

When I see my valuation for a lot, I compare it directly to the standing bid. If the standing bid is already at or above my valuation, I pass immediately—don't chase.

When the standing bid is well below my valuation, I bid aggressively in round 1 to establish control. A 25-30% raise above the minimum signals strength and discourages further bidding.

In round 2, if I'm still in contention for a lot worth significantly more to me than the current bid, I raise to secure it. This is my last chance, so I bid confidently rather than with the minimum raise.

When I win a lot, I track my remaining budget carefully. Know exactly what I have left for the remaining lots. After each win, subtract the final bid amount from my remaining budget, not from a fresh starting point. Errors in budget accounting compound across multiple lots and lead to overspending on later ones.

I don't bid just because a lot is worth something to me relative to the estimate. The estimate doesn't matter—only my valuation matters relative to what I'm actually paying. A lot worth 45 to me at a bid of 3 is good; the estimate of 33 is irrelevant.

I watch what other bidders are winning. If one bidder is accumulating most of the lots, that's not my problem—I focus on value for myself, not on "balancing the score."

On the final lot, if it represents good value relative to my remaining budget and my valuation, I bid to win it. Don't leave value on the table just because it's the last round.

I avoid the mistake of chasing lots where the current bid has already exceeded my valuation. Walking away cleanly preserves budget for better opportunities and prevents me from overpaying.

When a lot is worth substantially more to me than the standing bid in round 1, I bid decisively but not recklessly. Raising 25-30% above minimum is sufficient to signal strength; I don't need to raise excessively. This keeps my bids proportionate and preserves budget for remaining lots.

In round 2, bid to my valuation or slightly above if it's the final chance. Don't exceed my valuation just because I'm committed to winning. If the standing bid is already close to my valuation, a minimum raise is appropriate and still wins if no one else contests it.

When I have high remaining budget and multiple valuable lots ahead, I can afford to bid confidently but still shouldn't overpay. The goal is profit (value gained minus price paid), not just winning lots.

Even when the standing bid is low and the lot is worth a lot to me, verify my actual remaining budget before bidding. Don't assume my budget matches my opening budget minus recent wins—recalculate from the system output.

In round 2, if the standing bid is close to my valuation, a minimum raise can be sufficient to win. A small margin of profit is still profit. Don't feel obligated to bid aggressively when the math is already working in my favor.
